🏠 Re-Privatizing Fannie and Freddie: Don’t Introduce New Risks — Fix Housing Affordability First

Bill Ackman’s push to re-privatize Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — releasing them from conservatorship, restructuring or forgiving Treasury’s senior preferred stock, easing capital rules, and handing greater control to private shareholders — sounds like reform. It is not. In the current environment, it would privatize gains while leaving taxpayers with the downside, all without fixing what is driving the housing crisis.

Fannie and Freddie play a vital role as government-sponsored enterprises. They buy conforming loans (up to the current baseline limit of $832,750 in areas like Berks and Chester Counties in Pennsylvania), securitize them into mortgage-backed securities, and guarantee timely payment of principal and interest. This government-backed assurance, backed by real estate collateral, provides essential liquidity and keeps U.S. mortgage rates lower and more stable than a purely private market would deliver.

Since the 2008 bailout of roughly $191 billion, the GSEs have remitted well over $300 billion to taxpayers through dividends, sweeps, and guarantee fees (currently around 65 basis points). The system has been a net revenue generator while delivering systemic stability.

❌ The Real Source of the Housing Crisis

After spending time talking with real estate agents, home builders, and local housing professionals here in Chester County, one thing is clear: America’s housing affordability crisis is the direct result of two intersecting policy failures.

First, high conforming loan limits now support government-backed financing for homes approaching or exceeding $1 million. Second, excessive regulatory costs — zoning restrictions, lengthy permitting, environmental mandates, impact fees, and construction requirements — make it far more profitable for builders to focus on these larger, high-end homes instead of smaller, affordable starter or retirement units.

This combination severely distorts the market. New home construction has lagged long-term demand, remaining well below the levels needed to keep pace with population growth and household formation. As a direct consequence, most people in their twenties and thirties are effectively squeezed out of homeownership altogether. This is why first-time buyers now average around 40 years old in Pennsylvania.

💰 Leave the GSEs Alone — Fix Affordability First
Rather than rushing re-privatization and introducing new risks into an already unbalanced system that heavily favors million-dollar homes, we should leave Fannie and Freddie in their current conservatorship structure. The existing hybrid model provides proven liquidity and taxpayer returns. Changing it now would risk higher borrowing costs or weaker safeguards without addressing root causes.

🏠  Instead, policymakers should focus aggressively on the affordability crisis:

✅ Targeted lower rates for starter homes: The Federal Reserve should implement policies that deliver meaningfully lower interest rates specifically for smaller, entry-level homes (for example, those priced at or below the local median). This would help rebalance incentives away from luxury properties and make homeownership more accessible for younger families.

In fact, I have argued that 0% rate, fee-only loans up to the median home price (about $400K) that amortize over 10-15 years is what is needed to fix the market. The Federal Reserve could do this without new government consent to better achieve its dual mandates of low inflation and high employment, but Congress should be proactive in this regard. We should remember that the Federal Reserve provided near-zero rates for a long time, but the main beneficiaries were asset managers and wealthy investors — not average American families — since it was untargeted. But if the Federal Reserve targeted support for homes below median cost, it would be transformative and beneficial not just for young people but also for older folks and retirees. In other words, the Federal Reserve needs to use the same 0% QE tool it has in the past, but just in a targeted way.

✅ Attack regulatory barriers head-on: Slash zoning restrictions, streamline permitting, reduce unnecessary mandates, and lower construction-related costs at the local, state, and federal levels. These changes would encourage builders to construct the smaller starter and retirement homes that families actually need, increasing overall supply where it matters most.

Housing finance is inherently cyclical. Maintaining the current GSE backstop as a public good prevents localized problems from becoming national crises. But we cannot keep subsidizing million-dollar homes with taxpayer-backed guarantees while regulatory barriers block affordable construction for everyone else. Fix the supply distortions and rate misalignments first.

Only then will the system truly serve American families rather than high-end developers and investors. The housing market and younger Americans deserve solutions that expand opportunity, not experiments that shift more risk onto taxpayers. Keeping Fannie and Freddie stable while directly tackling regulatory barriers and delivering lower rates for starter homes is the practical way forward.
